message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"6c908a6964219e7f817f13e70fd1abf5160df10ddd9d47c3db9d668c4c861265","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nj-class-d:lineage:92","source_registry_sha256":"057b72c7c679c997f56ae00ef97a6b14dbe264551f4121b9bf67b0457d9cf7c1","units":[{"unit_id":"sec14-u01","module_id":"sec14-m01","objective_ids":["sec14-u01"],"title":{"text":"Title and register first","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-F02","sec14-R07"]},"why_how":[{"text":"A newly bought vehicle must be titled, registered and insured before it is driven on public roads.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01"]},{"text":"Newcomers have a deadline, and the paperwork has set pieces: application, ownership proof and sales tax.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03","sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-F07"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Sam moves to New Jersey with a car whose out-of-state registration runs out in thirty days.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Sam has sixty days to title and register, or sooner if the old registration runs out first.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03"]},"result":{"text":"Because the old registration runs out first, Sam titles and registers within those thirty days.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking any friend or relative can process your title and registration.","fact_ids":["sec14-R07"]},"correction":{"text":"Only the titled owner, or someone authorized to act for the owner, may process the transaction.","fact_ids":["sec14-R07"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Title, register, insure, then drive.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Sam moved here and the out-of-state registration ends in thirty days. What is Sam's deadline to title and register?","fact_ids":["sec14-F03"]},"answer":{"text":"Thirty days, because the old registration runs out before sixty days.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03"]},"rationale":{"text":"The newcomer deadline is sixty days, or sooner if the out-of-state registration runs out first.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec14-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Before the car moves","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-R07","sec14-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Title, register, insure.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-R07","sec14-F03"]},{"text":"Owners handle the paperwork.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-R07","sec14-F03"]},{"text":"Newcomers have sixty days.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-R07","sec14-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers the paperwork side of owning a vehicle in New Jersey. Before a resident drives a newly bought vehicle on public roads, whether it is new or used, it has to be titled, registered and insured. We will look at who is allowed to process that paperwork, what changes for leased and financed vehicles, how long a driver who moves here has to title and register, which application is used, how ownership and sales tax are proven, and how long a registration lasts. Each step is simple, but the order matters: the vehicle is not driven until all three are in place.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-R07","sec14-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Who handles the paperwork","fact_ids":["sec14-R07","sec14-R08","sec14-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Titled owner or authorized person.","fact_ids":["sec14-R07","sec14-R08","sec14-F02"]},{"text":"Leased: power of attorney.","fact_ids":["sec14-R07","sec14-R08","sec14-F02"]},{"text":"Lemon Law status on the title.","fact_ids":["sec14-R07","sec14-R08","sec14-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Only the titled owner, or someone authorized to act for the owner, may process a title and registration transaction at an MVC Vehicle Center. Leased vehicles add a step. A leased vehicle needs a power of attorney issued by the leasing company, and for a leased or financed vehicle coming from another state, you get the original title from the lien holder or leasing company. One more title rule: a vehicle classified under the Lemon Law must carry that classification on its title. So the title is more than a receipt; it records who may act for the vehicle and important facts about it.","fact_ids":["sec14-R07","sec14-R08","sec14-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The newcomer deadline","fact_ids":["sec14-F03","sec14-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Sixty days to title and register.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03","sec14-F01"]},{"text":"Sooner if old registration ends.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03","sec14-F01"]},{"text":"Applies to drivers moving in.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03","sec14-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"A driver who moves to New Jersey must title and register the vehicle within sixty days, or sooner if the out-of-state registration runs out first. That second part is where people slip. Sixty days is the outer limit, not a guarantee. If your old registration expires in three weeks, three weeks is your real deadline. So when you move, check the expiration date on your out-of-state registration right away. Compare it with sixty days from your move, and plan for whichever comes first. A resident who buys a vehicle here has no grace period at all: it is titled, registered and insured before it is driven.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03","sec14-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Application, ownership and tax","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"BA-forty-nine at a Vehicle Center.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-F07"]},{"text":"Certificate of origin, or signed title.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-F07"]},{"text":"Show or pay sales tax.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"An initial registration uses the BA-forty-nine application at an MVC Vehicle Center, and it must list the current insurance company and policy number. You also prove ownership. For a new vehicle, that is the manufacturer's certificate of origin plus the dealer's certificate of sale. For a used vehicle, it is a title signed over by the previous owner. Finally, you must show that sales tax has been paid, or pay it at an MVC Vehicle Center. Put together, the visit needs an application with insurance details, proof that the vehicle is yours, and proof that the tax is settled.","fact_ids":["sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Four years or one year","fact_ids":["sec14-F04","sec14-F16"]},"lines":[{"text":"Brand-new first registration: four years.","fact_ids":["sec14-F04","sec14-F16"]},{"text":"Other registrations: usually one year.","fact_ids":["sec14-F04","sec14-F16"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a timing trap. The first registration of a brand-new vehicle lasts four years, while other registrations usually last one year. A question might describe a used car and suggest a four-year registration, or describe a brand-new car and suggest one year. Ask two things: is the vehicle brand-new, and is this its first registration? Only when both are true does the four-year period apply. Every other registration usually runs one year. Do not confuse this four-year registration with the five-year dealer inspection sticker on new passenger vehicles, which you will meet in the inspection lesson.","fact_ids":["sec14-F04","sec14-F16"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the newcomer clock","fact_ids":["sec14-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Moved to New Jersey.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03"]},{"text":"Old registration ends in thirty days.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03"]},{"text":"Which deadline applies?","fact_ids":["sec14-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: Sam moves to New Jersey from another state. Sam's car is still registered in the old state, and that registration runs out in thirty days. Sam assumes there are sixty days to title and register the car here. What is Sam's real deadline? Work it out before reading on. Sam has thirty days. The rule gives a driver who moves to New Jersey sixty days to title and register, or sooner if the out-of-state registration runs out first. Here the old registration runs out first, so it sets the earlier deadline, and Sam should finish the paperwork before it expires.","fact_ids":["sec14-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Title and registration recap","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-R07","sec14-R08","sec14-F03","sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-F07","sec14-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Title, register, insure first.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-R07","sec14-R08","sec14-F03","sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-F07","sec14-F04"]},{"text":"Sixty days or sooner.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-R07","sec14-R08","sec14-F03","sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-F07","sec14-F04"]},{"text":"New car: four-year first registration.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-R07","sec14-R08","sec14-F03","sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-F07","sec14-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us review. A resident's newly bought vehicle, new or used, is titled, registered and insured before it is driven on public roads. Only the titled owner or an authorized person may process the transaction, and a leased vehicle needs a power of attorney from the leasing company. A driver moving in has sixty days, or less if the old registration runs out first. The BA-forty-nine application lists your insurer and policy number, ownership is proven with a certificate of origin and sale or a signed-over title, and sales tax is shown or paid. A brand-new vehicle's first registration lasts four years.","fact_ids":["sec14-F01","sec14-R07","sec14-R08","sec14-F03","sec14-F05","sec14-F06","sec14-F07","sec14-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec14-u02","module_id":"sec14-m02","objective_ids":["sec14-u02"],"title":{"text":"Plates: placement and care","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-F10"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Plates identify the vehicle, so where they go and how they are lit is set by rule.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-F10"]},{"text":"Lost, stolen, fake or unused plates each have their own required steps.","fact_ids":["sec14-F12","sec14-F13","sec14-F14"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Jordan sells a car, ends its insurance and is not buying another vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec14-F14"]},"reasoning":{"text":"When the vehicle is sold and no replacement is planned, the plates must be turned in to the MVC.","fact_ids":["sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]},"result":{"text":"Jordan surrenders the plates in person or by mail and keeps the receipt.","fact_ids":["sec14-R09"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a reflectorized rear plate needs no light at night.","fact_ids":["sec14-F10"]},"correction":{"text":"The rear plate must be lit so it can be read from fifty feet at night, even when it is reflectorized.","fact_ids":["sec14-F10"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Twelve to forty-eight up, fifty-foot light.","fact_ids":["sec14-F09","sec14-F10"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Jordan sold the car, ended its insurance and is not buying another. What happens to the plates?","fact_ids":["sec14-F14"]},"answer":{"text":"They must be turned in to the MVC.","fact_ids":["sec14-F14"]},"rationale":{"text":"Plates are turned in when insurance ends or the vehicle is sold with no plan to buy another; plates not transferred are surrendered with a receipt kept.","fact_ids":["sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec14-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Your license plates","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-F10","sec14-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"How many and where.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-F10","sec14-F12"]},{"text":"Lighting and covers.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-F10","sec14-F12"]},{"text":"Lost, fake or unused plates.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-F10","sec14-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"License plates are how a vehicle is identified on the road, so New Jersey sets clear rules for them. In this lesson we cover how many plates each type of vehicle gets, how high passenger plates are mounted, how the rear plate must be lit, and why a cover that hides lettering is a problem. Then we turn to plates that go wrong: lost or stolen plates, forged or counterfeit plates, and plates you no longer need. You will also learn when plates can move to your next vehicle and when they go back to the MVC. Keep the numbers for height and lighting separate as you go.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-F10","sec14-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Number and placement","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-R10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Cars: two matching plates.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-R10"]},{"text":"Trailer, moped, motorcycle: one.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-R10"]},{"text":"Twelve to under forty-eight inches.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-R10"]}],"narration":{"text":"A registered car gets two matching plates, one for the front and one for the rear, while a trailer, moped or motorcycle gets just one. For passenger vehicles, plates must be mounted at least twelve inches but less than forty-eight inches above the ground, and they must be kept clean and visible. Only valid plates may be placed on a vehicle. So picture a car with a matching plate at each end, both mounted within that height window and kept clean enough to read. A motorcycle, moped or trailer carries a single plate instead of a pair.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-R10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Lighting and covers","fact_ids":["sec14-F10","sec14-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Rear plate lit at night.","fact_ids":["sec14-F10","sec14-F11"]},{"text":"Readable from fifty feet.","fact_ids":["sec14-F10","sec14-F11"]},{"text":"Hidden lettering: fine up to one hundred dollars.","fact_ids":["sec14-F10","sec14-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"The rear plate must be lit so it can be read from fifty feet at night, and that is true even when the plate is reflectorized. Covers and holders matter too. A plate cover or holder that hides any lettering on the plate is a violation, with a fine of up to one hundred dollars. Notice the word any. A frame that covers only a small line of lettering still counts. The goal behind both rules is the same: anyone behind you should be able to read your plate, day or night, without anything blocking or dimming it.","fact_ids":["sec14-F10","sec14-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u02-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Inches versus feet","fact_ids":["sec14-F09","sec14-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Mounting: twelve to under forty-eight inches.","fact_ids":["sec14-F09","sec14-F10"]},{"text":"Lighting: readable from fifty feet.","fact_ids":["sec14-F09","sec14-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Two plate numbers sit close together and use different units. Mounting height is measured in inches: at least twelve inches but less than forty-eight inches above the ground. Lighting is measured in feet: the rear plate must be readable from fifty feet at night. A question may offer fifty inches as a mounting height, or twelve feet as a reading distance. Neither matches the manual. Tie inches to where the plate sits on the car, and feet to how far away someone must be able to read it in the dark. Reflectorized plates still need the light.","fact_ids":["sec14-F09","sec14-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u02-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Lost, stolen or fake plates","fact_ids":["sec14-F12","sec14-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Tell police, keep the complaint.","fact_ids":["sec14-F12","sec14-F13"]},{"text":"Tell MVC; replace lost plates in a day.","fact_ids":["sec14-F12","sec14-F13"]},{"text":"Counterfeit plates: fines, jail, suspension.","fact_ids":["sec14-F12","sec14-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"If plates are lost or stolen, report it to local police, retain a copy of the complaint and inform the MVC, and replace lost or damaged plates within twenty-four hours at any MVC Vehicle Center. Fake plates are treated harshly. Using forged or counterfeit plates can bring a fine of up to five hundred dollars, up to sixty days in jail, or a license suspension of up to six months. So the honest response to a missing plate is fast and documented, while any attempt to use a plate that is not genuine carries serious penalties, including possible jail time.","fact_ids":["sec14-F12","sec14-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u02-s6","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Turning in or transferring","fact_ids":["sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Insurance ends: turn plates in.","fact_ids":["sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]},{"text":"Sold with no replacement: turn in.","fact_ids":["sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]},{"text":"Most plates can transfer.","fact_ids":["sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Plates do not simply stay with you forever. If you end the vehicle's insurance, or the vehicle is sold, junked or destroyed and you do not plan to buy another, the plates must be turned in to the MVC. If you are buying another vehicle, most plates can be transferred to your next vehicle. Plates that are not transferred after a sale must be surrendered to the MVC in person or by mail, and you should keep the receipt. So after a sale you have two paths: move the plates to your next vehicle, or return them and keep proof that you did.","fact_ids":["sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u02-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the plates","fact_ids":["sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Car sold.","fact_ids":["sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]},{"text":"Insurance ended.","fact_ids":["sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]},{"text":"No new car planned.","fact_ids":["sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: Jordan sold a car, ended its insurance, and has no plans to buy another vehicle. Jordan's plates are sitting in the garage. What must happen to them? Work it out before reading on. They must be turned in to the MVC. The rule says plates are turned in when you end the vehicle's insurance, or when the vehicle is sold, junked or destroyed and you do not plan to buy another. Jordan can surrender them in person or by mail and should keep the receipt. Transferring would only make sense if Jordan were buying another vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u02-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Plates recap","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-R10","sec14-F10","sec14-F11","sec14-F12","sec14-F13","sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Two plates for cars.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-R10","sec14-F10","sec14-F11","sec14-F12","sec14-F13","sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]},{"text":"Twelve to forty-eight inches, fifty feet.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-R10","sec14-F10","sec14-F11","sec14-F12","sec14-F13","sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]},{"text":"Turn in or transfer.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-R10","sec14-F10","sec14-F11","sec14-F12","sec14-F13","sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us review. A car gets two matching plates, and a trailer, moped or motorcycle gets one. Passenger plates sit at least twelve inches but less than forty-eight inches above the ground, kept clean and visible, and only valid plates may be used. The rear plate is lit so it can be read from fifty feet at night, even if reflectorized, and a cover that hides any lettering can bring a fine of up to one hundred dollars. Lost or stolen plates are reported to police and the MVC while lost or damaged plates are replaced within twenty-four hours, counterfeit plates bring serious penalties, and unused plates are turned in or transferred.","fact_ids":["sec14-F08","sec14-F09","sec14-R10","sec14-F10","sec14-F11","sec14-F12","sec14-F13","sec14-F14","sec14-R09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec14-u03","module_id":"sec14-m03","objective_ids":["sec14-u03"],"title":{"text":"Inspection schedules","fact_ids":["sec14-F15","sec14-F16","sec14-R02"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Inspection timing depends on the vehicle's fuel, use and age.","fact_ids":["sec14-F15","sec14-F17","sec14-R03"]},{"text":"New vehicles start with a dealer sticker instead of an inspection.","fact_ids":["sec14-F16","sec14-R02"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Taylor owns a gasoline passenger car that is eight model years old and a gasoline commercial van.","fact_ids":["sec14-F15","sec14-F17"]},"reasoning":{"text":"The passenger car is inspected every two years, while the commercial van is inspected every year.","fact_ids":["sec14-R01"]},"result":{"text":"Taylor schedules the van every year and the car every two years.","fact_ids":["sec14-R01"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking every vehicle follows the same two-year inspection schedule.","fact_ids":["sec14-R01"]},"correction":{"text":"Covered commercial vehicles are inspected every year; the two-year schedule is for passenger vehicles.","fact_ids":["sec14-R01","sec14-F17"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Passenger two, commercial one.","fact_ids":["sec14-R01"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Taylor's gasoline commercial van is three years old. How often must it be inspected?","fact_ids":["sec14-F17"]},"answer":{"text":"Every year.","fact_ids":["sec14-F17"]},"rationale":{"text":"Gasoline commercial vehicles must be inspected every year, while passenger vehicles covered by the rule go every two years.","fact_ids":["sec14-F17","sec14-R01"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec14-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"When inspections are due","fact_ids":["sec14-F15","sec14-F17","sec14-F16"]},"lines":[{"text":"Passenger vehicles: every two years.","fact_ids":["sec14-F15","sec14-F17","sec14-F16"]},{"text":"Commercial vehicles: every year.","fact_ids":["sec14-F15","sec14-F17","sec14-F16"]},{"text":"New vehicles: dealer stickers.","fact_ids":["sec14-F15","sec14-F17","sec14-F16"]}],"narration":{"text":"New Jersey inspects vehicles on schedules that depend on what the vehicle is and how old it is. In this lesson we compare the passenger vehicle schedule with the commercial vehicle schedule, look at the dealer stickers that new vehicles receive instead of an early inspection, and cover the separate rule for diesel passenger vehicles. The numbers here are easy to swap, especially the two-year and one-year intervals and the five-year and one-year stickers. As you go, ask three questions about any vehicle: is it passenger or commercial, what fuel does it use, and how many model years old is it?","fact_ids":["sec14-F15","sec14-F17","sec14-F16"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Passenger vehicles and new stickers","fact_ids":["sec14-F15","sec14-F16"]},"lines":[{"text":"Gasoline, model year nineteen ninety-six on.","fact_ids":["sec14-F15","sec14-F16"]},{"text":"More than five model years old.","fact_ids":["sec14-F15","sec14-F16"]},{"text":"Inspected every two years.","fact_ids":["sec14-F15","sec14-F16"]}],"narration":{"text":"Gasoline-fueled passenger vehicles from model year nineteen ninety-six on that are more than five model years old must pass a state inspection every two years. Newer vehicles start differently. New passenger vehicles under five model years old receive a new car dealer sticker that expires five years after initial registration. So a passenger car's life has two phases: first the dealer sticker, then, once it is more than five model years old, a state inspection every two years. The sticker is separate from the registration and marks a new passenger vehicle that is not yet due for inspection.","fact_ids":["sec14-F15","sec14-F16"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Commercial and diesel rules","fact_ids":["sec14-F17","sec14-R03","sec14-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"Commercial gasoline: every year.","fact_ids":["sec14-F17","sec14-R03","sec14-F15"]},{"text":"Light diesel commercial: every year.","fact_ids":["sec14-F17","sec14-R03","sec14-F15"]},{"text":"Diesel passenger: every two years.","fact_ids":["sec14-F17","sec14-R03","sec14-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"Commercial vehicles are on a tighter schedule. Gasoline-fueled commercial vehicles, and diesel commercial vehicles with a gross vehicle weight rating of eight thousand five hundred pounds or less, must be inspected every year. Diesel passenger vehicles have their own rule. Those from model year nineteen ninety-seven on, more than five model years old and with a gross vehicle weight rating of eight thousand five hundred pounds or less, must pass an emissions inspection every two years. Notice the model years differ: nineteen ninety-six for the gasoline passenger rule, nineteen ninety-seven for the diesel passenger rule.","fact_ids":["sec14-F17","sec14-R03","sec14-F15"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec14-u03-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Two years, one year, five years","fact_ids":["sec14-R01","sec14-R02","sec14-F16"]},"lines":[{"text":"Passenger inspection: every two years.","fact_ids":["sec14-R01","sec14-R02","sec14-F16"]},{"text":"Commercial inspection: every year.","fact_ids":["sec14-R01","sec14-R02","sec14-F16"]},{"text":"Stickers: five years versus one year.","fact_ids":["sec14-R01","sec14-R02","sec14-F16"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Passenger vehicles are inspected every two years, but commercial-registered vehicles covered by the rule are inspected every year. Stickers follow a similar split.
